meta.title: One Map, Any Key
meta.summary: Five shapes, learned once and filled in over five chapters, now cover the whole neck in any key — and the closing account of what that does and does not buy you.

spans.text: Five shapes. That's the whole inventory, and it was the whole inventory from the first lesson of this pathway.
Chapter 1 handed the five forms over as windows with a root or two lit inside each one. Chapter 2 put the third and the fifth in. Chapter 3 added the
and the
. Chapter 4 added the
and the
, and this chapter moved between the windows, walked along them, ran chords through them, and carried the whole thing to another key. At no point was a sixth shape asked for.
The Root Ladder
promised exactly that, and it's now fully paid. Five shapes, four layers, and one chapter of connecting them — that's the entire pathway, not four separate ones.
Five forms, five chapters, one shape learned once. Everything since chapter 1 was the same five windows filling in — never a new one.
What You Can Do Now

items.text: Find any root of any major chord anywhere on the neck.
Say which degree is under any finger, in any form.
Play the whole major scale in any position.
Cross from one window into the next without stopping, through a note both windows own.
Play up a single string instead of across the neck.
Put a progression wherever your hand already is, instead of jumping back to the nut.
Move all of it to another key, because the ladder itself never changes — only where you enter it.

spans.text: None of those on their own were the point of any single chapter — each came from stacking one layer on top of the last, on windows that never changed shape underneath.
The Honest Limits
A closer that only celebrates isn't trustworthy, so here's the other side of it, stated as plainly as the wins above.

Everything in this pathway has been major: major chords, the major scale, five major forms. Minor chords, seventh chords, and the rest of harmony are a different map laid over the same neck. The habit you've built — root first, then degrees, then the window around them — is the habit that reads those maps too. The maps themselves are not in this pathway, and pretending otherwise would be doing you no favours.

And the criticism this chapter opened with is only half answered by knowing the map. Knowing that a doorway exists between two windows is not the same as your hand finding it at speed, without looking, mid-phrase. The other half of that criticism is hours on the instrument, not another lesson — a map tells you where the road goes, it doesn't drive you there.
What to Practise
Four things, drawn straight from this chapter and nothing beyond it, so the list stays usable instead of exhaustive:

items.text: One octave up a single string, low E or high e, through all five windows — the drill that proved you can't be boxed in if you're on a string.
string-pair run from fret 3 to fret 10, root to root — the version people actually play.
— played in two different places without going back to the nut.
The whole ladder in one key that isn't
— start on the letter you already play best as an open chord.

spans.text: Where to Go From Here
The articles stop here, but the app doesn't. Four screens, each for a different job than the ones this pathway's diagrams could do:
Scale Visualizer
puts all five windows live on the neck, in any key, with the CAGED position toggle and the same form names you've been using this whole pathway.
Drone
gives you a sustained root to play a window against — the quickest way to hear whether a note arrives home or just leans on the way past.
Chord Shapes
answers the question this pathway's diagrams never did: of everything lit in a window, which notes a hand can actually hold at once.
Chord Detector
listens back — play a form somewhere unfamiliar and check that what comes out is the chord you meant.

One last picture, in the one key this chapter uses that has no open chord of its own: five bands, same order, same overlaps, and not one of them an open shape. If you can read this cold, you can read it in any key — which is exactly the point of closing on
F
rather than
C
The boxes were never the point. They were how the neck got small enough to learn.
